title: India calls for a shift from Drought Response to Drought Resilience at UNCCD CoP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia
subtitle:
Treat Drought as a Predictable and Preventable Risk, Not a Recurring Disaster: Shri Bhupender Yadav
Preparedness over Response, Prevention over Crisis Management, Resilience over Recovery should be the Goal: Union Environment Minister
body_text:
Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, today called for a fundamental shift in the global approach to drought - from reactive relief to proactive, technology-enabled resilience. Addressing the Ministerial Dialogue on ‘Accelerating Drought Resilience’, at the 17th Conference of Parties (CoP17) of the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), in Ulaanbaatar (Mongolia), the Minister said drought is “no longer an occasional event, but a defining development challenge”, affecting water security, food systems, biodiversity and economic stability.
Shri Yadav highlighted India’s coordinated, multi-institutional approach integrating early warning, mitigation, relief and community resilience. Rainfall monitoring and satellite-based drought assessments trigger preparedness at the inter-ministerial and State levels, ensuring that a dry spell does not escalate into a crisis. Emphasising the critical link between land and water, he stated, “restore the forest, before the flow”, underscoring India’s focus on catchment and riverscape forestry to reduce erosion, improve water retention and recharge groundwater. River rejuvenation and revival of traditional water bodies further strengthen water security and rural drought resilience.
The Minister highlighted that community-led restoration of springs and recharge zones in India's hills, while in the plains, a pan-India watershed programme addresses degraded rainfed lands through a ridge-to-valley approach, supported by community institutions and convergence with rural employment programmes. At the household level, drinking water programmes seek to ensure reliable supplies during periods of stress, with assured service levels, local quality testing and prioritisation of vulnerable areas. He also highlighted crop insurance that protects farmers against drought and other non-preventable losses across the crop cycle, combining subsidised premiums with technology-driven assessment for faster and transparent claim settlement. The Minister stressed that community ownership, capacity building and livelihood diversification are central to the transition from reactive relief to proactive, technology-enabled resilience.
Shri Yadav said India’s core belief is that “drought must be managed as a predictable, preventable risk, and not a recurring disaster demanding emergency response”. He highlighted prevention measures including watershed development, water harvesting, afforestation, groundwater recharge and climate-resilient crops, complemented by disaster-related funds, employment guarantees, fodder support and emergency water supplies when required. Calling for stronger global action, Shri Yadav advocated greater investment in ecosystem restoration, stronger early warning systems and coordinated action. “Preparedness over response, prevention over crisis management, resilience over recovery should be the goal”, he said. He concluded by emphasizing that building drought resilience is not optional for the world’s most vulnerable, but a matter of survival, and affirmed India’s readiness to share its knowledge and capacities, including on early warning, for a drought-resilient future for all.

ministry.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

enrichment.summary: At UNCCD CoP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav called for a global shift from reactive drought relief to proactive, technology-enabled drought resilience. He outlined India's multi-institutional approach combining early warning systems, watershed development, river and spring rejuvenation, groundwater recharge, drinking water programmes, and crop insurance to build resilience against drought. He urged greater global investment in ecosystem restoration and early warning systems, framing drought as a predictable, preventable risk rather than a recurring disaster.
enrichment.context:
The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), one of the three Rio Conventions (alongside UNFCCC and CBD), addresses land degradation, desertification and drought, with its Conference of Parties (CoP) meeting periodically to review global action. Drought resilience has gained prominence as climate change intensifies water stress worldwide, and UNCCD has been pushing member states toward a proactive 'drought preparedness' paradigm rather than post-disaster relief, including through frameworks like the Integrated Drought Management Programme.

India's drought management architecture draws on several existing schemes referenced in the speech: the Watershed Development Component under PMKSY (ridge-to-valley approach), the Jal Jeevan Mission (household drinking water assurance), the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (crop insurance with technology-driven claim settlement), MGNREGA (convergence for livelihood and water conservation works), and river rejuvenation efforts like Namami Gange. This speech consolidates India's existing policy narrative for an international audience rather than announcing new schemes, but it is useful for understanding India's stated position and framework on drought and desertification at a global forum.

prelims_questions.explanation: The three Rio Conventions arising from the 1992 Earth Summit are UNFCCC, CBD, and UNCCD. CITES is a separate treaty on wildlife trade, not a Rio Convention.
